title: Cognitive Load Theory: The Story of a Research Programme https://www.researchgate.net/publication/294106592_Story_of_a_Research_Program
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), October 21, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers John Sweller's scholarly autobiography tracing the origins and evolution of Cognitive Load Theory, from his early experiments through the discovery of its landmark effects. Sweller recounts how conventional problem-solving, especially the means-ends analysis strategy students default to, heavily overloads the limited capacity of working memory and blocks the transfer of new knowledge into long-term memory — the core insight that launched decades of research. He walks through the theory's major discoveries: the worked-examples effect (studying examples beats solving the same problems from scratch), the split-attention effect, the redundancy effect, the modality effect, and the expertise-reversal effect, which flips the advice for advanced learners once worked examples become redundant. Barton frames this as Sweller's own account of persistently challenging the dominant constructivist paradigm over a career, with the through-line being that explicit instruction, not minimal guidance, is what the cognitive architecture of learning actually supports for complex material.
points: Conventional problem-solving, especially the means-ends analysis strategy students default to, heavily overloads working memory and blocks new knowledge from transferring into long-term memory.

The worked-examples effect — learners who study worked examples outperform those who solve the same problems from scratch — was one of CLT's founding discoveries and remains a core classroom implication.

The expertise-reversal effect means worked examples that help novices become redundant or even counterproductive for advanced learners, who should shift to problem-solving practice or partially-completed problems as they gain expertise.

Sweller frames his career as a sustained challenge to the dominant constructivist paradigm, arguing that cognitive architecture favors explicit instruction over minimal guidance for biologically secondary (curriculum) knowledge.
quotes: The worked example effect demonstrated clearly that showing learners how to do something was far better than having them work it out themselves.

The research suggests that conventional problem solving, particularly using a means-ends analysis strategy, heavily overloads the limited capacity of working memory, preventing the transfer of knowledge to long-term memory (learning).
Teachers should leverage the Worked Examples Effect, where learners who study worked examples perform better on test problems than those who solve the same problems themselves.

For advanced learners (experts), worked examples can become redundant; teachers should introduce problem solving practice or completion problems (partially completed problems) as learners gain expertise (Expertise Reversal Effect).
Teachers should explicitly show students how to solve problems rather than expecting them to discover the knowledge themselves through minimal guidance.
